content: 1. Neisseria meningitidis has emerged as a leading cause of bacterial meningitis in the United States, following significant reductions in the incidence of Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) infections due to the use of conjugate vaccines. 2. The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) of the CDC previously recommended a tetravalent polysaccharide vaccine (Menomune® A, C, Y, W-135) for individuals aged 11–55 years. 3. ACIP now recommends routine vaccination of young adolescents (ages 11–12) with the quadrivalent meningococcal conjugate vaccine (MCV4) during their preadolescent healthcare visit. 4. Introducing MCV4 vaccination for young adolescents may enhance the importance of the preadolescent healthcare visit and improve vaccine coverage among adolescents. 5. For individuals who have not previously received MCV4, ACIP recommends vaccination before high school entry (around age 15) as an effective strategy to reduce meningococcal disease incidence among adolescents and young adults. 6. By 2008, the goal is to achieve routine MCV4 vaccination for all adolescents starting at age 11. 7. Vaccination is also recommended for military recruits, travelers to hyperendemic or epidemic areas, microbiologists exposed to Neisseria meningitidis isolates, patients with anatomic or functional asplenia, and those with terminal complement deficiencies. 8. Other groups, such as college students, adolescents, and individuals with HIV who wish to reduce their risk of meningococcal disease, may elect to receive the vaccine. 9. This report updates previous ACIP recommendations on the prevention and control of meningococcal disease, including updated guidance on the use of the tetravalent meningococcal polysaccharide vaccine (MPSV4) and antimicrobial chemoprophylaxis. 10. Neisseria meningitidis colonizes the mucosal surfaces of the nasopharynx and is transmitted through direct contact with large droplet respiratory secretions from patients or asymptomatic carriers. Humans are the only known host. 11. Despite the availability of effective antibiotics, including penicillin, the case-fatality rate for meningococcal disease remains 10%–14%. Survivors may experience severe complications such as neurologic disability, limb loss, or hearing loss. 12. In the United States, most cases of meningococcal disease are sporadic, but localized outbreaks have increased since 1991. Serogroups B, C, and Y are the primary causes of meningococcal disease, each accounting for approximately one-third of cases. 13. Among infants, serogroup B causes over 50% of cases, but no licensed vaccine is available for this serogroup in the United States. For individuals aged >11 years, 75% of cases are caused by serogroups C, Y, or W-135, which are included in available vaccines. 14. Persons with terminal complement pathway deficiencies (C3, C5–C9) or anatomic/functional asplenia are at increased risk for meningococcal disease. Other risk factors include antecedent viral infections, household crowding, chronic illnesses, and exposure to tobacco smoke. 15. During outbreaks, behaviors such as bar or nightclub attendance and alcohol use have been associated with higher risk for meningococcal disease. 16. College students, particularly those living in dormitories, are at moderately increased risk for meningococcal disease compared to their peers. Vaccination and educational programs targeting this population are recommended. 17. Outbreaks of meningococcal disease have occurred with increasing frequency in the United States since the early 1990s. These outbreaks are often caused by serogroups C, B, or Y and may occur in community or organizational settings. 18. Vaccination campaigns are a key strategy for controlling outbreaks, but decisions to vaccinate depend on the attack rate and whether the cases represent an outbreak or endemic clustering. 19. Mass chemoprophylaxis is generally not recommended for controlling large outbreaks due to logistical challenges, cost, potential side effects, and the risk of antimicrobial resistance. 20. Meningococcal polysaccharide vaccines are safe and effective but have limitations, including poor immunogenicity in young children, lack of long-lasting immunity, and inability to reduce nasopharyngeal carriage or interrupt transmission. 21. Conjugate vaccines, which link polysaccharides to protein carriers, overcome many limitations of polysaccharide vaccines by inducing T-cell-dependent immune responses, providing long-lasting immunity, and reducing bacterial carriage. 22. The introduction of conjugate vaccines for Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) and Streptococcus pneumoniae has significantly reduced disease incidence and provided herd immunity by reducing asymptomatic carriage. 23. In the United Kingdom, monovalent serogroup C conjugate vaccines were introduced in 1999, leading to a substantial reduction in serogroup C meningococcal disease.
